strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: First last-iterate convergence proof to Nash equilibrium for the unregularized game in LLM alignment, achieving robust alignment (50% win rate)
Elegant unifying framework: Shows PPO, DPO, IPO, INPO and other methods implement the prox operator, enabling black-box integration into meta-algorithm
Sound technical analysis: Rigorous proofs of convergence with proper treatment of approximation errors (Theorem 3)
Clear synthetic validation: Figure 2 convincingly demonstrates COMAL converges while IPO/SPPO diverge cyclically, validating theoretical predictions
Well-motivated problem: Addresses genuine limitation that existing methods either diverge, have only average-iterate convergence, or converge to modified KL-regularized game losing robust alignment
weaknesses: Insufficient LLM experiments: Only one small model (Qwen2-1.5B) and single dataset (UltraFeedback) tested, limiting generalizability claims
Unfair computational comparisons: COMAL trains for 42 iterations while baselines run 3-6 iterations. Lacks comparison with INPO/IPO at equal computational budget—critical control experiment

Gap between theory and practice: Theorem 1 assumes exact prox computation; Theorem 3 requires approximation error εₜ ≤ c₁²/(9t⁴) with problem-dependent constants never verified empirically during training
Unclear practical importance: Paper doesn't empirically show cyclic preferences actually occur in human preference datasets. The motivating problem may not be practically relevant
Strong unverified assumptions: Assumption 1 (supp(π*) = supp(πsft)) not guaranteed and may be violated; no discussion of what happens when violated
Vague hyperparameter adaptation: Reference policy update criterion ('when optimization begins to converge') lacks principled guidance and appears post-hoc based on hyperparameter search
Modest empirical improvements: ~5-10% win rate gains with substantially higher computational cost; INPO plateau in Figure 3 may indicate overfitting rather than fundamental divergence
Same oracle for data generation and evaluation: Doesn't test generalization; preference oracle noise/bias robustness untested

strengths: First last-iterate convergence guarantee to unregularized Nash equilibrium in LLM alignment (not KL-regularized versions), advancing over concurrent work like INPO and Nash-MD
Elegant unifying framework showing many existing methods (PPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, INPO) can be interpreted as prox operators
Complete theoretical analysis covering both exact and approximate solutions with well-structured proofs
Practical integration with existing methods requires minimal modifications (demonstrated via Algorithm 4 with INPO)
Comprehensive related work positioning against concurrent approaches
weaknesses: Critical gap between theory and practice: Theory requires exact prox solutions or ε_t ≤ c₁²/(9t⁴), but experiments use only 3 SGD epochs with batch size 32; no verification that approximation bounds are satisfied

Insufficient experimental validation: Single small model (Qwen2-1.5B) on one dataset (UltraFeedback); marginal improvements (COMAL 60.90% vs INPO-Small 59.16%, ~1.7 points); no human evaluation; no statistical significance testing

Questionable practical impact: Computational cost of solving regularized game at each iteration not analyzed; no wall-clock time comparisons; unclear if robust alignment property (50% win rate against any policy in restricted space Π) is practically important
Restricted applicability: Nash equilibrium guarantee only within Π = {π : supp(π) ⊆ supp(π_sft)}, preventing novel responses; significantly limits generality
Ad-hoc implementation details: Reference policy update criterion ('when first optimization step begins to converge') is vague and unprincipled; limited guidance on setting regularization parameter τ
Limited theoretical novelty: Results primarily apply standard prox-method analysis from Nemirovski (2004); main contribution is application to LLM alignment rather than new mathematical insights
Missing critical ablations: No sensitivity analysis on τ, no analysis of K_t requirements, no comparison of different prox implementations, no ablation showing reference policy updates are necessary
Presentation issues: Convoluted connection between Algorithms 1-4; dense mathematical exposition obscures core algorithm; practical Algorithm 4 receives minimal treatment

strengths: Solid theoretical contribution: Proves last-iterate convergence to Nash equilibrium (Theorem 1), stronger than prior average-iterate results, with extension to approximate solutions
Elegant algorithmic design: Unifies multiple existing algorithms (PPO, DPO, IPO, INPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO) through Prox operator interpretation, enabling flexible black-box integration
Well-motivated problem: Addresses genuine limitation of Bradley-Terry assumption; robust alignment guarantee (≥50% win rate) is well-defined and meaningful
Comprehensive experimental design: Synthetic experiments clearly demonstrate algorithmic convergence properties; LLM experiments extended to 42 iterations with structured evaluation
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with good motivation, algorithm descriptions, and comprehensive appendices including additional methods and hyperparameter studies
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 assumes exact solution to regularized game, but Algorithm 4 uses inexact INPO with manually-defined stopping criteria ('when convergence/overfitting begins') that lacks theoretical formalization

Limited scope of LLM experiments: Only one model size (1.5B), single dataset (UltraFeedback), learned preference oracle instead of human preferences, no error bars/confidence intervals; generalizability severely limited
Computational cost unaddressed: COMAL requires 42 meta-iterations × hundreds of inner steps vs. ~3 for INPO; no wall-clock time comparison provided despite being critical for practical adoption
Modest practical improvements: COMAL achieves 60.90% vs INPO-Small's 59.16% (~1.7% absolute gain); unclear if improvement justifies computational overhead without significance testing
Incomplete comparisons: Mirror-Prox and OMWU algorithms deferred to future work despite both achieving last-iterate convergence; more thorough comparison with Nash-MD needed
Regularization parameter selection lacks principled guidance: τ manually adjusted based on observed convergence; no ablation studies on sensitivity or guidance for practitioners
Assumption 1 justification insufficient: Requires Nash equilibrium matching SFT support; no empirical verification in experiments or discussion of failure modes
Iterate averaging criticism hand-wavy: Dismisses averaging as compute-inefficient without detailed analysis; post-training averaging could address concerns

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution: Last-iterate convergence to exact Nash equilibrium (Theorem 1) and extension to approximate solutions (Theorem 3), advancing beyond average-iterate guarantees
Valuable unifying insight: Shows existing preference optimization algorithms (DPO, IPO, INPO, etc.) implement the prox operator, enabling integration with minimal changes
Clear problem motivation: Effectively articulates limitations of Bradley-Terry assumptions and motivates general preference framework
Comprehensive experimental validation: Synthetic experiments clearly demonstrate convergence where baselines diverge; LLM experiments on multiple models with standard benchmark checks
Thorough documentation: Extensive appendices with multiple algorithm variants, detailed proofs, and practical implementations demonstrating generality
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Asymptotic convergence only (no finite-time rate); Theorem 2 bound O(1/ε²) requires rapidly decaying error tolerances; no provable guarantees in non-convex LLM settings (acknowledged in Section L). Critical gap between theoretical Nash equilibrium guarantees and actual LLM behavior

Experimental design concerns: (1) Preference oracle uses mixture of Bradley-Terry models, contradicting general preference motivation; (2) Unfair comparisons: Iter-IPO/INPO at best checkpoints (iter 6) vs COMAL at final checkpoint (iter 18); (3) Closed-loop evaluation using same oracle for training and testing masks robustness issues

Modest empirical improvements: ~10-15% win rate gains over INPO are consistent but not dramatic; standard benchmarks (Table 3) show minimal or negative improvements; no statistical significance testing provided

Limited validation of Nash equilibrium properties: No systematic verification that final LLM models achieve >50% win rate against arbitrary policies as theoretically guaranteed. LLM experiments don't directly validate Nash equilibrium achievement

Ad-hoc hyperparameter tuning: Dynamic variation of η⁻¹ (0.002 to 0.1), τₜ, Kₜ across iterations undermines simplicity claims; unclear if baselines received equal tuning effort; no ablation studies on key design choices like reference policy update frequency

strengths: Solid theoretical contributions with last-iterate convergence to Nash equilibrium and results for approximate solutions (Theorem 3) that improve upon prior work requiring exact solutions
Comprehensive framework showing how diverse existing methods (DPO, IPO, INPO, SPPO, REBEL) can be interpreted as computing prox operators, providing useful unification
Extensive experimental evaluation across multiple model sizes and standard benchmarks with detailed ablations in appendices
Consistent improvements showing >60% and 56% win rates against compared algorithms in controlled settings
weaknesses: Critical motivation-reality gap: Paper claims to handle general (non-BT) preferences but experiments use mixture of two BT models as preference oracle, which itself relies on Bradley-Terry assumptions; synthetic intransitive preference experiments are disconnected from main LLM experiments

Significant theory-practice gap: Theorems assume convexity; LLM training is non-convex. Theorem 3 requires knowing unknowable problem-dependent constants and iteration-dependent approximation errors that are difficult to verify in practice

Modest empirical improvements: Only ~2% win rate improvement over best baseline (INPO: 60.2% vs 57.89%) on main task; inconsistent performance on standard benchmarks (Table 3 shows Iter-IPO better on Arena-Hard)

Substantial hyperparameter tuning burden with model-dependent settings: η⁻¹ changed from 0.002 to 0.1 after iteration 6 for Llama-3; reference policy update frequency selected ad-hoc; different settings needed for different models without principled guidance
Flawed evaluation protocol: Using same preference oracle for both training and evaluation does not test generalization; no evaluation on true non-BT general preferences despite being core motivation
Missing critical ablations: No systematic study of reference policy update frequency, τ sensitivity, or outer vs. inner iteration trade-offs
Concurrent work (Wang et al., 2025) appears to achieve similar results; unique advantages over Magnetic Mirror Descent approach not clearly articulated

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution: First algorithm with provable last-iterate convergence to exact Nash equilibrium in alignment game (Theorem 1), even with approximate solutions (Theorem 3), surpassing prior work
Well-motivated problem: Clear articulation of Bradley-Terry limitations and effective motivation for general preference models using intuitive examples
Practical and modular design: Demonstrates integration with multiple existing preference optimization methods (DPO, IPO, INPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, etc.) with minimal modifications
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive experiments across synthetic games, multiple LLM sizes (1.5B-8B), and standard benchmarks with appropriate baselines
Unifying perspective: Insightful interpretation of diverse preference optimization methods through the prox operator lens
Detailed reproducibility: Thorough algorithmic descriptions and hyperparameter documentation enabling reproduction
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Convergence guarantees assume convex preferences and apply to non-convex losses only heuristically; Assumption 1 (support preservation) may not hold during training
Modest empirical improvements: Win-rate gains over strong baselines are 3-5% (60.25% vs 62.98% for INPO-L); standard benchmark results show no consistent advantage
Inconsistent results: COMAL underperforms Iter-IPO on Arena-Hard (41.3% vs 43.8%, Table 3), contradicting theoretical superiority claims
Preference oracle still structured: Experiments use mixture of BT models rather than truly general preferences; unclear generalization to arbitrary preference distributions
Experimental setup concerns: Evaluation with same preference oracle as training is circular; 'best checkpoint' selection varies by method, complicating fair comparison
Incremental algorithmic novelty: Core algorithm is application of conceptual prox method (Nemirovski 2004) to LLM alignment; main insight is recognizing existing methods compute prox operator
Heuristic hyperparameter choices: Manual η^{-1} schedule (0.002→0.1) and π_ref update criteria lack principled justification; sensitivity analysis missing
Unclear practical significance: Connection between maintaining 50% Nash equilibrium win rate and downstream task performance not established
